title: Quiz: PCA for Dimensionality Reduction and Cluster Visualisation

questions.text: The eigenvalue λₖ associated with principal component k represents:
options: The number of original variables most correlated with PCk
The variance of the data when projected onto the direction of PCk
The proportion of total variance explained by PCk
The correlation between PCk and the outcome variable
questions.explanation: The eigenvalue λₖ is the variance of the data projected onto the eigenvector direction vₖ. The proportion of variance explained is λₖ / Σλ, not the eigenvalue itself. Larger eigenvalues mean the corresponding PC captures more variance.

questions.text: You have 5 variables with eigenvalues 3.0, 1.5, 0.8, 0.4, 0.3. What proportion of variance is explained by the first two PCs?
In a biplot, a long arrow for the variable 'num_claims' pointing strongly in the positive PC1 direction means:
options: num_claims has a large positive loading on PC1 and strongly influences that component
num_claims is negatively correlated with PC1
num_claims has a small variance relative to other variables
num_claims is the most important variable for predicting the outcome
questions.explanation: In a biplot, the length of an arrow indicates the magnitude of the variable's loading on the displayed PCs. A long arrow in the positive PC1 direction means that high values of num_claims correspond to high PC1 scores — num_claims is a strong driver of PC1.

questions.text: You call prcomp(data_scaled, scale. = TRUE) but your data is already Z-score standardised. What happens?
options: An error is thrown because scale. = TRUE requires unscaled data
The data is standardised a second time — each variable is divided by 1, which has no effect
The already-scaled variables (all sd ≈ 1) are re-scaled by 1/1 = 1 — effectively no change, so results are correct
The covariance matrix is replaced by the correlation matrix
questions.explanation: scale. = TRUE divides each column by its standard deviation before computing PCA. If the data is already standardised, each column's sd ≈ 1, so dividing by 1 changes nothing. However, it is cleaner to set scale. = FALSE when the data is already scaled to avoid double-standardisation in edge cases.

questions.text: If two k-means clusters overlap in a PC1 vs. PC2 scatter plot, this proves that the clustering algorithm failed to find meaningful groups.
questions.explanation: k-means operates in the full p-dimensional feature space. The PCA plot projects this onto 2D, potentially losing 15-30% of variance. Clusters that are separated in dimensions 3, 4, or 5 may appear to overlap in the 2D projection. Overlap in 2D does not imply clustering failure — check silhouette scores and cluster profiles.

questions.text: Principal components are guaranteed to be orthogonal to each other. What practical benefit does this provide in a downstream regression model?
options: Orthogonal predictors have zero correlation, so there is no multicollinearity in a regression on PCs
Orthogonal predictors always have equal variance
Orthogonal components always sum to zero
Regression on PCs is always more accurate than regression on raw variables
questions.explanation: Multicollinearity occurs when predictors are highly correlated. Because PCs are orthogonal (uncorrelated by construction), a regression on PCs has zero multicollinearity, making coefficient estimates stable and interpretable. This is the basis of principal components regression (PCR).
